newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Payrolls in the spotlight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK -- Payrolls in the spotlight.

text.p: U.S. credit market players on Friday will pore over key jobs data, hoping to unearth more facts to fuel a recent rally in Treasuries, experts said. Pundits polled by Reuters, on average, predicted the U.S. economy added 211,000 non-farm payroll jobs in April after gaining 175,000 in March.
The figures are due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
The employment report comes as bulls, who recently pushed the yield on the benchmark 30-year bond below 7.0 percent, are preparing for next week's $29 billion sale of Treasury notes.

"With that background we've got a problem because we've broken through a pretty important level and you really need to continue to get good news that will suggest that yields can go much lower," said Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co International Inc.
Brusca said an extra large gain in payrolls or other good news for the economy "could really set the bond market back."
"It's particularly vulnerable during these refunding cycles," he added.
The Treasury plans to sell $17 billion in three-year notes next Monday and $12 billion in 10-year notes on Tuesday.

Economists expected the April jobless rate to hold steady at 5.2 percent, the average work week to shrink to 34.7 hours in April from 34.8 hours in March and average hourly earnings to rise 0.3 percent after increasing 0.4 percent previously.
Average hourly earnings have been steadily inching higher since last November. Yet analysts doubted a 0.3 percent gain would send inflation jitters through the markets.

"The higher it is the more disturbing it (will) be, but unless it's really a number other than three tenths or four tenths, I don't think it will have a major impact on the market," said Charles Lieberman of Chase Securities Inc.
The Chase Securities' chief economist noted that average hourly earnings is not as accurate a measure of labor costs as the employment cost index (ECI).
On Tuesday, the U.S. Labor Department reported that the ECI rose 0.6 percent in the first quarter, a weaker gain than the 0.9 percent increase that was expected in a Reuters poll.
The benign ECI and a surprising 3.0 percent drop in March durable goods orders had sent Treasuries soaring and the yield on the long bond tumbling below 7.0 percent.
April employment data are expected to overshadow other economic reports set for release later in the day.

Other data scheduled for release on Friday include the Economic Cycle Research Institute (ECRI) monthly future inflation gauge due out at 1025 EDT/1425 GMT and the Center for International Business Cycle Research (CIBCR) leading inflation index expected at 1040 EDT/1440 GMT.
Both will report their April readings. In March, the ECRI stood at 110.0 and the CIBCR was at 105.8.
In late trading, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 18/32 at 96.12/32 to yield 6.91 percent.
